svg.title: Full fuel or full seats: trading payload against fuel
svg.desc: Invented example. Maximum gross weight 2,550 pounds minus basic empty weight 1,500 pounds is a useful load of 1,050 pounds. Full fuel of 53 gallons at 6 pounds per gallon is 318 pounds, leaving 732 pounds for people and baggage. Four adults weighing 760 pounds do not fit with full fuel, so fuel is cut to about 290 pounds, 48 gallons: 1,500 plus 760 plus 288 is 2,548 pounds, just under the maximum. Fuel for the trip and required reserves comes first, and the CG must be checked again after any change.
svg.text: Full fuel or full seats: trading payload against fuel
Invented example: maximum gross weight 2,550 lb, basic empty weight 1,500 lb, so the useful
The 1,050 lb useful load is shared between fuel and people and bags (drawn to scale)
Full fuel: 53 gal x 6 lb = 318 lb
Room for 732 lb of people and baggage
Four adults: 760 lb, so fuel is cut to 290 lb (48 gal)
1,500 + 760 + 288 (48 gal) = 2,548 lb, under the 2,550 lb maximum gross weight
Useful load = maximum gross weight - basic empty weight. Fuel counts against it: gasoline is
Each lb of fuel you add takes a lb of room away from people and bags, and the other way round
Fuel for the trip and the required reserves comes first (14 CFR 91.151). If it will not fit
with the people, shorten the leg or leave someone or something behind
Any change in the load moves the CG. Work out the new CG, not only the weight
Source: PHAK (FAA-H-8083-25C) ch. 10, Weight and Balance; 14 CFR 91.151 (fuel reserves). Numbers
